cases.question: What does the Nigeria Small Business Tax Act 2025 say about turnover limits?

claims.text: The Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 defines a "small business" as a business that earns gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less per annum with a total fixed assets less than ₦250,000,000, provided that any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small business.

The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 defines a "small company" as a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000, provided that any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company.

"Gross turnover" means the gross inflow of economic benefits during the period arising in the course of the operating activities of an entity when those inflows result in increases in equity, including sales of goods, supply of services, receipt of interest, rents, royalties or dividends, other than increases relating to contributions from equity participants.

In determining whether a person meets the threshold of being a small company, the value of the supply of a capital asset of the person is excluded from taxable supplies. The value of a supply made solely as a consequence of the person selling the whole or a part of its business or permanently ceasing to carry on business is also excluded.

</question>
<gaps>

cases.rendered:
The Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 defines a "small business" as a business that earns gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less per annum with a total fixed assets less than ₦250,000,000, provided that any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small business. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business"]

The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 defines a "small company" as a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000, provided that any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

"Gross turnover" means the gross inflow of economic benefits during the period arising in the course of the operating activities of an entity when those inflows result in increases in equity, including sales of goods, supply of services, receipt of interest, rents, royalties or dividends, other than increases relating to contributions from equity participants. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "gross turnover"]

In determining whether a person meets the threshold of being a small company, the value of the supply of a capital asset of the person is excluded from taxable supplies. The value of a supply made solely as a consequence of the person selling the whole or a part of its business or permanently ceasing to carry on business is also excluded. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not include any Act called the "Nigeria Small Business Tax Act 2025"; the turnover limits above come from the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 and the Nigeria Tax Act 2025.

- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business" (gazette page A 331)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "gross turnover" (gazette pages A 504, A 505)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10) (gazette page A 277)

- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": A small business has gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less in the cited print and ₦50,000,000 or less in the Gombe print. (DR-267)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": Total fixed assets must be less than ₦250,000,000 in the cited text and not more than ₦250,000,000 in the National Assembly text, so exactly ₦250,000,000 qualifies only under the National Assembly text. (DR-270)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 59 (gazette page A 427)

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)

cases.question: I filed my company's VAT return three months late. What is the total penalty?

claims.text: A taxable person who fails or refuses to file returns, or knowingly files incomplete or inaccurate returns, to the relevant tax authority in accordance with the Act is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦100,000 in the first month in which the failure occurs.
The same provision adds an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 for each subsequent month in which the failure continues.
Where any tax is not paid within the period prescribed under the Act, a sum equal to 10% of the amount of the tax payable is added to it, subject to section 67 of the Act.

Unpaid tax also carries interest from the date it becomes payable until it is paid. For naira remittances, the rate is the prevailing monetary policy rate of the Central Bank of Nigeria plus a spread determined by the Minister.

For foreign currency remittances, interest on unpaid tax is at the prevailing Secured Overnight Financing Rate ("SOFR") or any successor rate, plus 10% or such other spread as the Minister determines.
The interest under section 65(1)(b) and (c) is compound interest.
The penalty and interest under section 65 are not deemed part of the tax paid for the purpose of claiming relief under the Act or any other tax law.

cases.rendered:
A taxable person who fails or refuses to file returns, or knowingly files incomplete or inaccurate returns, to the relevant tax authority in accordance with the Act is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦100,000 in the first month in which the failure occurs. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 101]

The same provision adds an administrative penalty of ₦50,000 for each subsequent month in which the failure continues. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 101]

Where any tax is not paid within the period prescribed under the Act, a sum equal to 10% of the amount of the tax payable is added to it, subject to section 67 of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

Unpaid tax also carries interest from the date it becomes payable until it is paid. For naira remittances, the rate is the prevailing monetary policy rate of the Central Bank of Nigeria plus a spread determined by the Minister. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

For foreign currency remittances, interest on unpaid tax is at the prevailing Secured Overnight Financing Rate ("SOFR") or any successor rate, plus 10% or such other spread as the Minister determines. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

The interest under section 65(1)(b) and (c) is compound interest. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

The penalty and interest under section 65 are not deemed part of the tax paid for the purpose of claiming relief under the Act or any other tax law. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say which return is a VAT return or whether section 101 applies to VAT returns specifically.
- The total in naira needs a calculation of the monthly penalties, which is not done here.
- Whether any tax was also unpaid, and the amount of any unpaid tax, is not stated, so the 10% addition and interest cannot be worked out.
- Section 67 of the Act, which section 65(1) is subject to, is not among the passages.
- The spread set by the Minister is not among the passages.
- How to count the months (whether three months late means the first month plus two subsequent months) is not stated in the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 101 (gazette page A 312)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65 (gazette pages A 298, A 299)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65: Interest is SOFR plus 10% or such other spread as the authority determines in the cited text; the National Assembly text says SOFR plus a spread to be determined, without the 10%. (DR-243)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65: Only the cited text makes the interest in subsection (1)(b) and (c) compound and applies it to tax debts unpaid at commencement. (DR-245)

This is a research and reference tool. It is not tax advice and is not a substitute for a licensed tax professional. It must not be used for an actual filing or compliance decision. Answers come only from the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and selected parts of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 (Official Gazette text, corpus snapshot 18 October 2026).

cases.question: We sold a warehouse for ₦150 million that cost us ₦90 million, and we never claimed capital allowance on it. How much tax is due on the gain?

claims.text: Where capital allowance has not been made in accordance with the First Schedule, the chargeable gain is determined by deducting from the disposal proceeds the amount or value of the consideration, in money or money's worth, incurred wholly and exclusively for the acquisition of the asset.
This computation of gains is stated to be subject to other provisions of the Act.

Where capital allowance has been made under the First Schedule on an asset used for a trade, business, profession or vocation, only the residue of that asset is deducted from the disposal proceeds when computing chargeable gains.

Where a trade or business sells or transfers a business asset without ceasing, for an amount not exceeding the sum of the residue of the qualifying capital expenditure and unutilised capital allowance of the asset, the chargeable gains provisions of Part VIII of Chapter Two do not apply to that asset.

gaps: The rate of tax on a chargeable gain is not among the passages.

There is no further tax charged on a dividend received by a non-resident from a Nigerian company, other than tax deducted at source under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 19]

Nothing in the Nigeria Tax Act gives the non-resident, or the Nigerian company paying the dividend, a right to repayment of tax paid under section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 19]

A Nigerian dividend is the gross amount of the dividend distributed by a Nigerian company, before any deduction. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 7]

A Nigerian company includes a company formed, registered or incorporated under any law in Nigeria, or one whose central or effective place of management or control is Nigeria. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "Nigerian company"]

- The passages do not say whether the Netherlands parent is a non-resident person under the Act.

The VAT rate is in section 148 of the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, headed "Rate of VAT". It says that, subject to the provisions of Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act, VAT is charged on the value of all taxable supplies at the rate of 7.5%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 148]

Section 154 tells a taxable person making taxable supplies to collect VAT at the rate specified in section 148. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 154]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, to which section 148 is made subject, is not among the passages.

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 148 (gazette page A 472)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 154 (gazette page A 474)

cases.rationale: ntaa2025:s72 subsections (2) to (4): banks and government bodies demand a certificate for the three years before the current year of assessment for the listed transactions.
cases.question: Why would my bank ask for a tax clearance certificate, and how many years must it cover?

claims.text: Any Ministry, department or agency of Government or any commercial bank that a person deals with on any of the transactions listed in subsection (4) shall demand from that person a tax clearance certificate of three years immediately preceding the current year of assessment.

The transactions listed are: application for certificate of occupancy; approval of building plans; application for award of contract by government or its agencies; application for firearms licence; application for import and export licence; and application for trade licence.

A tax clearance certificate shall disclose, for the last three years of assessment, the total profits or chargeable income, tax payable, tax paid, and tax outstanding or alternatively a statement that no tax is due.

The relevant tax authority shall issue a certificate within two weeks of the demand if it is of the opinion that the assessed tax has been fully paid or that no tax is due, or otherwise give reasons for the denial.

gaps: The passages do not say which specific dealing with a bank (for example, a particular account, loan or service) the question refers to, so whether the bank's request falls under the listed transactions cannot be confirmed.

cases.rendered:
Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. In the case of a small company, the rate is 0%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

A small company is a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Separately, where a company's effective tax rate in a year of assessment is less than 15%, it shall recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%. This applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The question's text says small companies pay 5%, but the passages do not state that figure. The rate in the passages is as set out in the claims above.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

Furniture and Fittings Expenditure is in Class 2 of Table I, with a rate of 20%.

Where a person has incurred qualifying expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of its trade or business, an allowance is made for each year of assessment in the basis period for which the asset was used for that trade or business, at the rate specified in Table I.
A capital allowance for a year of assessment is made if, at the end of a basis period, the person is the owner of the asset and used it for the purposes of its trade or business.
Where the basis period for a year of assessment is less than one year, the allowance for that year is granted proportionately.
The residue of a qualifying expenditure is the total qualifying expenditure incurred on or before the date, less the total capital allowance made before that date.
Where the owner uses the asset only partly for a trade or business, the allowance is apportioned to the trade or business as may be reasonable.

An allowance shall not be made for a year of assessment unless it is claimed for that year, or where the relevant tax authority is of the opinion that it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to do so.

An allowance is subtracted from the remainder of the assessable profits or income for the relevant year, and any part that cannot be fully deducted because there is no remainder or an insufficient remainder is treated as a deduction for the next year and succeeding years until fully utilised.

gaps: The yearly amount needs a calculation applying the Class 2 rate to the cost and to the residue, which is not done here.
The passages do not say whether the rate applies to the original cost or to the residue each year.
Whether the furniture is used wholly for the business, and the length of the basis period, are not stated.

An allowance shall not be made for a year of assessment unless it is claimed for that year, or where the relevant tax authority is of the opinion that it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to do so. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 21 to 22]

claims.text: A taxable person must, not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, remit the excess to the Service where output VAT exceeds input VAT.
Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, the taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months.
Output VAT is the VAT a taxable person collects on making taxable supplies, and input VAT is the VAT a taxable person pays to a supplier on a taxable supply made to it.

A taxable person must submit a VAT return to the Service in the prescribed form, on or before the 21st day of the following month. The return must contain the input tax paid, output tax collected and VAT payable on all taxable supplies in the preceding month.
If the Service grants an extension of the time for filing the return, that does not extend the time to pay the tax.
The VAT filing rule in subsection (1) does not apply to a small business.

Input tax may be deducted only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in making taxable supplies. Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to taxable supplies may be deducted.

The passages do not say whether the business is a taxable person or a small business.

cases.rationale: ntaa2025:s65 subsection (1): 10% of the tax added plus interest at the CBN monetary policy rate plus a spread set by the Minister; the spread is not in corpus and no amount may be computed.
cases.question: We paid ₦3 million of company tax 45 days late. How much extra do we owe in penalty and interest?

claims.text: Where any tax is not paid within the period prescribed under the Act, a sum equal to 10% of the amount of the tax payable is added to it. This is subject to section 67 of the Act.

For naira remittances, the unpaid tax carries interest at the prevailing monetary policy rate of the Central Bank of Nigeria plus a spread to be determined by the Minister. It runs from the date the tax becomes payable until it is paid.

For foreign currency remittances, the unpaid tax incurs interest at the prevailing Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) or any successor rate, plus 10% or such other spread as the Minister determines. It runs from the date the tax becomes payable until it is paid.
The interest under section 65(1)(b) and (c) is compound interest.
The penalty and interest under section 65 are not treated as part of the tax paid when claiming relief under the Act or any other tax law.
The relevant tax authority may, for good cause shown, remit the whole or any part of a penalty or interest due under the Act or any other tax law.

gaps: The amounts of the Central Bank of Nigeria monetary policy rate, the Minister's spread and, for foreign currency, the SOFR are not in the passages, so the interest figure cannot be worked out.
The calculation of the 10% sum and of compound interest over the late period is not done here.
Section 67, which section 65(1) is made subject to, is not among the passages.
The passages do not say whether the tax was a naira or foreign currency remittance, or what the prescribed payment period was.

Section 104 deals with failure to use the fiscalisation system. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 104]

A taxable person that fails to process a taxable supply through the fiscalisation system is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦200,000 plus 100% of the tax due and an interest at the prevailing Central Bank of Nigeria Monetary Policy rate per annum. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 104]

A taxable person means a person who carries out economic activity in a place, or a person exploiting tangible or intangible property for the purpose of obtaining income from it by way of trade or business, or an agency of Government acting in that capacity. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "taxable person"]

Tax includes any duty, levy or other revenue accruable to the Government in full or in part under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025, or any other law. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "tax"]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say what the fiscalisation system is or how a taxable supply is processed through it.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.rationale: ntaa2025:s73(1)-(4): advance rulings on application by a taxable person, issued within 21 days or with written reasons.
cases.question: Can my company ask the tax service for a written ruling on how a law applies before we go ahead with a deal?

claims.text: The relevant tax authority may issue an advance ruling on an application by a taxable person within 21 days of receiving the application, or give written reasons for being unable to issue it.
The relevant tax authority means the Nigeria Revenue Service, or the Internal Revenue Service of a State or of the Federal Capital Territory in Nigeria.
An application must be made in the prescribed form and manner by a person who is a party to a tax related issue or transaction, or by two or more parties to it.

The definition of advance ruling covers a written opinion or decision given to a taxpayer by the relevant tax authority on a transaction, a proposed transaction or any tax matter, to give direction or clarification.

An application must contain the taxpayer's contact details, a complete description of the issue or transaction and its financial implications, if any, and a complete description of its possible impact on tax liability.

An application must also give details of any ongoing audit, previous correspondence and earlier decisions of the tax authority, the legal basis relied on, the reasons the ruling should be granted, and a written statement on whether the matter is before any tribunal or court of competent jurisdiction.

The relevant tax authority may ask the applicant for more information. Where necessary, it shall give the applicant a reasonable opportunity to make representations or clarifications. An applicant may withdraw the application at any time before a ruling is issued.

The relevant tax authority may reject an application that requires an opinion on foreign law, an issue already before a court or tribunal of competent jurisdiction, interpretation of the Constitution, an issue that is academic, hypothetical, frivolous or vexatious, or a ruling that will interfere substantially with an ongoing audit, investigation or other proceeding involving the applicant or connected persons.
A ruling is limited to the applicant and the transaction it is given for. It is rendered on a set of facts before the tax authority and cannot be of general application.

A ruling is void where the transaction actually carried out is materially different from the one described, where there is fraud, misrepresentation or non-disclosure of a material fact, or where an assumption or condition set by the tax authority is not satisfied or carried out by the taxpayer.
A ruling ceases to be effective if the tax law provision it concerns is repealed or amended in a way that materially affects it, or if a court overturns or modifies the interpretation it is based on.

<question>
Can my company ask the tax service for a written ruling on how a law applies before we go ahead with a deal?
</question>
<gaps>
<gap index="0">
The prescribed form and manner of application are not set out in the passages.
</gap>

cases.rendered:
The relevant tax authority may issue an advance ruling on an application by a taxable person within 21 days of receiving the application, or give written reasons for being unable to issue it. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(1) to (4)]

The relevant tax authority means the Nigeria Revenue Service, or the Internal Revenue Service of a State or of the Federal Capital Territory in Nigeria. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "relevant tax authority"]

An application must be made in the prescribed form and manner by a person who is a party to a tax related issue or transaction, or by two or more parties to it. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(1) to (4)]

The definition of advance ruling covers a written opinion or decision given to a taxpayer by the relevant tax authority on a transaction, a proposed transaction or any tax matter, to give direction or clarification. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "advance ruling"]

An application must contain the taxpayer's contact details, a complete description of the issue or transaction and its financial implications, if any, and a complete description of its possible impact on tax liability. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

An application must also give details of any ongoing audit, previous correspondence and earlier decisions of the tax authority, the legal basis relied on, the reasons the ruling should be granted, and a written statement on whether the matter is before any tribunal or court of competent jurisdiction. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

The relevant tax authority may ask the applicant for more information. Where necessary, it shall give the applicant a reasonable opportunity to make representations or clarifications. An applicant may withdraw the application at any time before a ruling is issued. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 73(5) to (8)]

The relevant tax authority may reject an application that requires an opinion on foreign law, an issue already before a court or tribunal of competent jurisdiction, interpretation of the Constitution, an issue that is academic, hypothetical, frivolous or vexatious, or a ruling that will interfere substantially with an ongoing audit, investigation or other proceeding involving the applicant or connected persons. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 74]

A ruling is limited to the applicant and the transaction it is given for. It is rendered on a set of facts before the tax authority and cannot be of general application. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 75]

A ruling is void where the transaction actually carried out is materially different from the one described, where there is fraud, misrepresentation or non-disclosure of a material fact, or where an assumption or condition set by the tax authority is not satisfied or carried out by the taxpayer. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 75]

A ruling ceases to be effective if the tax law provision it concerns is repealed or amended in a way that materially affects it, or if a court overturns or modifies the interpretation it is based on. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 75]

claims.text: Every person, including a company granted exemption from incorporation, shall maintain books or records of accounts, whether or not the person is liable to pay tax.
The books and records required to be maintained shall be in English language and, for the purpose of tax, shall be consistent with the format that may be prescribed by the relevant tax authority.

Where the record is maintained in a language other than the English language, the person shall, on demand by the tax authority, produce at its own expense a translation in English language, certified by a sworn translator.

A taxable person who fails to keep accounts, books and records of business transactions and income, to allow for the correct ascertainment of tax and filing of returns to the relevant tax authority, is liable to an administrative penalty; in the case of a company, the amount printed is ₦50,000.

The term "book" includes any register, document or other records of information and any account or accounting record, however compiled, recorded or stored, including in written, printed, micro-film, digital, magnetic or electronic form or otherwise.

gaps: The passages do not say whether keeping books in French, with an English translation produced on demand, counts as keeping them in English for the purposes of the penalty in section 102.
The passages do not say what format the relevant tax authority has prescribed for books and records.

Notes

The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 defines a small company as a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Gross turnover means the gross inflow of economic benefits during the period arising in the course of the operating activities of an entity when those inflows result in increases in equity, including sales of goods, supply of services, receipt of interest, rents, royalties or dividends, other than increases relating to contributions from equity participants. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "gross turnover"]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The question refers to the Nigeria Tax Act 2027. The passages concern the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 only, and no 2027 Act is among them.

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "gross turnover" (gazette pages A 504, A 505)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)

Tax charged by an assessment that is not the subject of an objection or appeal is payable at the place stated in the notice of assessment within 30 days of service of the notice on the taxable person. The relevant tax authority, in its discretion, may extend the time for payment. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Once an objection or appeal is determined, the relevant tax authority serves a notice of the tax payable as determined, and that tax is payable within 30 days of the date of service of that notice. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Where an objection or appeal has been given notice of, collection stays in abeyance until it is determined, but the taxable person pays the tax that is not the subject of the objection or appeal. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Every person pays tax due on or before the due date of filing, in one lump sum or in instalments. The final instalment is paid on or before the due date of filing. This is subject to section 11 of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

Where a trade, business, profession or vocation permanently ceases to carry on operations in Nigeria in an accounting period, the tax is payable within six months from the date of cessation. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 24]

After a demand notice is served, the relevant tax authority may proceed to enforce payment under the Act if payment is not made within 30 days from the date of service of the notice. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

A taxable person must submit a VAT return to the Service in the prescribed form on or before the 21st day of the following month, with or without a notice and whether or not an economic activity has taken place. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

A taxable person who fails or refuses to file returns, or knowingly files incomplete or inaccurate returns, to the relevant tax authority in accordance with the Act is liable to an administrative penalty of ₦100,000 in the first month in which the failure occurs and ₦50,000 for each subsequent month in which the failure continues. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 101]

If the Service grants an extension of the period for filing VAT returns, the extension does not extend the time to pay the tax. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

The VAT return filing rule in section 22(1) does not apply to a small business. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

Where tax is not paid within the prescribed period, a sum equal to 10% of the tax payable is added to it, and interest also runs on the tax due. This is subject to section 67 of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

A taxable person is a person who carries out economic activity in a place, a person exploiting tangible or intangible property to obtain income from trade or business, or a government agency acting in that capacity. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "taxable person"]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The question asks to use P2 only, but the penalty for late filing is stated in section 101, which is a different passage. Only the passages as supplied have been used.
- The question's text says late VAT returns attract no penalty in the first year of trading. No passage states this, so it is not treated as law.
- Section 67 of the Act, which section 65 refers to, is not among the passages.
- Whether the section 101 penalty applies to a late VAT return in particular is not stated; the passages do not link section 101 to section 22.
- The monetary policy rate and the spread set by the Minister are not among the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10) (gazette page A 277)

- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65: Only the cited text makes the interest in subsection (1)(b) and (c) compound and applies it to tax debts unpaid at commencement. (DR-245)

must_not: computed amount
claim that the gain is exempt under the ₦150 million proceeds threshold alone
cases.rationale: Shares are chargeable assets (nta2025:s34); the share exemption needs proceeds under ₦150,000,000 and a gain not over ₦10,000,000, so it does not cover this gain, but reinvestment relief (proviso (iii)) may, and is a material proviso (D-43(b)). Gain = proceeds less cost (nta2025:s39 paragraph (b)), included in total profits (nta2025:s27(1)-(4)), rate nta2025:s56.
cases.question: Our company sold shares in another Nigerian company for ₦60 million; we paid ₦25 million for them. What tax do we owe on that gain?

claims.text: All forms of property are chargeable assets for the purposes of the Part on chargeable gains, whether situated in Nigeria or not, and this includes shares. This is subject to exemptions that may be provided in Part I of Chapter Eight of the Act.

Gains accruing to a person on disposal of shares in any Nigerian company are not chargeable gains where the disposal proceeds, in aggregate, are less than ₦150,000,000 and the chargeable gain does not exceed ₦10,000,000 in any 12 consecutive months.

Gains on disposal of shares in any Nigerian company are also not chargeable gains where the proceeds are reinvested within the same year of assessment in the acquisition of shares in the same or other Nigerian companies, notwithstanding the threshold above. Gains on disposal of shares in any Nigerian company are also not chargeable gains where the proceeds are reinvested within the same year of assessment in the acquisition of shares in the same or other Nigerian companies, notwithstanding the threshold above. Tax accrues proportionately on the portion of the proceeds that is not reinvested. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 34]

Gains on disposal of shares in any Nigerian company are also not chargeable gains where the shares are transferred between an approved borrower and a lender in a regulated securities lending transaction. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 34]

A company may be charged to tax in its own name. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 5]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Whether the gain on this sale is chargeable depends on the size of the gain and on whether the proceeds were reinvested. Working out the gain from the sale price and cost is a calculation the passages do not do.

- How the gain is computed, including allowable deductions, is not among the passages.
- Part I of Chapter Eight of the Act, which section 34 refers to for exemptions, is not among the passages.

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 34 (gazette page A 416)

From the commencement of the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, the Companies Income Tax Act, Cap. C21, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004, is repealed. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 196]

The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 sets out how the total profits of a company are worked out for a year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4)]

Under the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, the Nigeria Revenue Service has exclusive responsibility to administer taxes on companies. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 3(1)]

The Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 sets filing times for company income tax returns, including not more than six months after the end of the accounting year for a company that has been in business for more than 18 months. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 11(3) to (6)]

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 196 (gazette pages A 498, A 499)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 412, A 413)

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 196: The gazette also repeals the Taxes and Levies (Approved List for Collection) Act; the National Assembly text does not. (DR-104)

cases.question: A consultant is offering us a scheme to cut our company tax bill. Do we have to tell the tax office about it?

claims.text: A person who enters or intends to enter into a transaction or agreement whose principal purpose is a benefit which enables, or might be expected to enable, that person to obtain a tax advantage shall, without notice or request, give the relevant tax authority information about it. The law calls this a disclosable transaction or agreement.

Tax advantage includes a relief or increased relief from tax, repayment or increased repayment of tax, avoidance or reduction of a charge to tax or an assessment to tax, avoidance of a possible assessment to tax, deferral of a payment of tax or advancement of a repayment of tax, and avoidance of an obligation to deduct or account for tax.
Transaction includes a course of action, agreement, scheme or arrangement.

The relevant tax authority may make regulations on the information to be provided, the form and manner of delivery, the time within which it is to be provided, and administrative penalties for non-disclosure, false disclosure, incomplete disclosure or late disclosure.

Separately, the relevant tax authority may counteract a prohibited tax avoidance arrangement by adjusting, disregarding or re-characterising it, in part or whole, unless the taxable person proves to the authority's satisfaction that granting the benefit would be in accordance with the object and purpose of the relevant provisions of the Act or any other tax law.

An arrangement is a prohibited tax avoidance arrangement where, having regard to the facts and circumstances, it is reasonable to conclude that its main purpose was to obtain a tax benefit or advantage, that obtaining the advantage is contrary to the object and purpose of the tax law, that it results directly or indirectly in misuse or abuse of the tax law, or that it lacks commercial substance or coherence in whole or in part.

<question>
Our catering company's turnover grew to ₦65 million this year, but our fixed assets are only ₦20 million. Are we still a small company for income tax?
</question>
<gaps>

cases.rendered:
A small company is defined as a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Tax on a company's total profits is levied at 0% for a small company and at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act for any other company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

Gross turnover means the gross inflow of economic benefits during the period arising in the course of the operating activities of an entity, when those inflows result in increases in equity, including sales of goods, supply of services, receipt of interest, rents, royalties or dividends, other than increases relating to contributions from equity participants. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "gross turnover"]

The Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 separately defines a small business as one earning gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets less than ₦250,000,000, again excluding any business providing professional services. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business"]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Whether the company's turnover is above the small company limit is a comparison of the question's figures with the definition, which the passages do not do for this company.
- The passages do not say whether a catering company counts as a business providing professional services.
- The passages do not say whether the turnover figure in the question matches the definition of gross turnover.
- The passages do not say whether the small business definition in the Tax Administration Act applies to the income tax rate question.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "gross turnover" (gazette pages A 504, A 505)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business" (gazette page A 331)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": A small business has gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less in the cited print and ₦50,000,000 or less in the Gombe print. (DR-267)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": Total fixed assets must be less than ₦250,000,000 in the cited text and not more than ₦250,000,000 in the National Assembly text, so exactly ₦250,000,000 qualifies only under the National Assembly text. (DR-270)

must_not: claim that an insurance payout is never taxed
computed amount
cases.rationale: An insurance sum for damage or loss of assets is a disposal (nta2025:s35 subsection (2)(b)). nta2025:s43: if applied within three years to a replacement, a chargeable gain arises when compensation plus scrap value exceeds the replacement cost; otherwise an additional asset for capital allowance. The three-year condition is material (D-43(b)).
cases.question: Our warehouse burnt down and the insurer paid us. If we use the money to build a replacement, is any of the payout taxed?

claims.text: Where an asset is lost or destroyed, and a capital sum received as compensation for the loss or destruction is applied within three years of receipt in acquiring another asset in its replacement, the owner is deemed to make a chargeable gain if the compensation together with the residual or scrap value is greater than the cost of the replacement asset.

If the compensation together with the residual or scrap value is lower than the cost of the replacement asset, the owner is deemed, for the purposes of the First Schedule, to have acquired an additional asset for an amount equal to the cost of the new asset less the compensation together with the residual or scrap value.
Except for that additional asset, allowance claimed on the new asset for the purposes of the First Schedule is limited to the residue of the old asset, if any.
A building means a structure permanently affixed to land for all or most of its useful life, and the definition includes a warehouse.

gaps: The passages do not say whether an insurance payout for a burnt warehouse counts as the capital sum received by way of compensation in section 43. A policy-of-insurance rule in section 49 is among the passages, but the passages do not link it to this payout.
The passages do not say whether building a replacement counts as acquiring another asset in replacement.
The passages do not give the amounts, the residual or scrap value, or the cost of the replacement, so whether a gain arises needs a calculation that is not done here.
The passages do not state the rate or the way tax on a chargeable gain is charged.

cases.rationale: A service consumed in Nigeria is a supply in Nigeria wherever rendered (nta2025:s146 paragraph (b)(i)); the Nigerian recipient withholds and remits the VAT (nta2025:s151 subsection (2)) unless an appointed collector has collected it (subsection (4)); rate nta2025:s148. cases.question: A firm in Ghana does our bookkeeping remotely. Do we have to deal with VAT on its fees?

claims.text: A taxable person pays VAT to a supplier on the taxable supply made to the person, and the VAT paid is known as input VAT.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom a taxable supply is made in Nigeria, and who is issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 is to be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction, or as may be prescribed by the Service.

The remission is to be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.

A person with an obligation to collect VAT under Chapter Six of the Act must keep proper records and make appropriate returns and remittances, and the compliance provisions apply to that person as though it is the taxable person.
Section 155 applies without prejudice to any provision of the Act or any other tax law.

gaps: The passages do not say whether bookkeeping services supplied remotely by a firm in Ghana are a taxable supply made in Nigeria.
The passages do not say whether the business is a taxable person, or whether the Service has directed it to self-account.
The passages do not say whether a foreign supplier must register for or charge VAT, or how a non-resident supplier is treated.

Where a liability or expenditure of a capital nature is waived, it is a chargeable gain for the purposes of Part VIII of Chapter Two of the Act.

cases.question: We run a bakery with yearly sales of about ₦80 million and equipment worth ₦30 million. Must we file VAT returns every month?

claims.text: A taxable person must submit a VAT return to the Service in the prescribed form on or before the 21st day of the following month, with or without a notice, and whether or not an economic activity has taken place.

A small business is a business that earns gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets less than ₦250,000,000.
A business providing professional services is not classified as a small business.

A small business may, by written notice to the Service, choose to opt out of the exemption given to small businesses, including registration, charging tax on taxable supplies and filing of returns. A business that ceases to be a small business shall file monthly VAT returns.

cases.rendered:
A taxable person must submit a VAT return to the Service in the prescribed form on or before the 21st day of the following month, with or without a notice, and whether or not an economic activity has taken place. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

The monthly filing rule in section 22(1) does not apply to a small business. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

A small business is a business that earns gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets less than ₦250,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business"]

A business providing professional services is not classified as a small business. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business"]

A small business may, by written notice to the Service, choose to opt out of the exemption given to small businesses, including registration, charging tax on taxable supplies and filing of returns. This option does not apply to companies engaged in petroleum operations as defined in the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

A business that ceases to be a small business shall file monthly VAT returns. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

In deciding whether a person meets the small company threshold, the value of supplying a capital asset of the person is excluded. So is the value of a supply made solely because the person sells the whole or part of its business or permanently stops carrying on business. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say whether a bakery's goods or sales count as taxable supplies or whether the bakery is a professional services business.
- Whether the bakery's turnover and the value of its equipment count as gross turnover and total fixed assets for the small business definition is not stated, and the comparison of the figures with the thresholds is left to the reader.
- The passages do not say whether the bakery has opted out of the small business exemption by written notice.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10) (gazette page A 277)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business" (gazette page A 331)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10): Cross-references: subsection (4), sections 105 and 107 (cited) against subsection (5), sections 100 and 102 (National Assembly). (DR-198)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 22(1) to (10): Cross-reference: section 152 of the Nigeria Tax Act (cited) against section 151 (National Assembly text, the same section under its numbering, DR-000). (DR-199)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": A small business has gross turnover of ₦100,000,000 or less in the cited print and ₦50,000,000 or less in the Gombe print. (DR-267)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 147, definition of "small business": Total fixed assets must be less than ₦250,000,000 in the cited text and not more than ₦250,000,000 in the National Assembly text, so exactly ₦250,000,000 qualifies only under the National Assembly text. (DR-270)

cases.rendered:
Where any tax is not paid within the period prescribed under the Act, a sum equal to 10% of the amount of the tax payable is added to it. This is subject to section 67 of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

For naira remittances, unpaid tax carries interest at the prevailing monetary policy rate of the Central Bank of Nigeria plus a spread to be determined by the Minister. It runs from the date the tax becomes payable until it is paid. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

For foreign currency remittances, unpaid tax incurs interest at the prevailing SOFR or any successor rate, plus 10% or such other spread as the Minister determines, from the date the tax becomes payable until it is paid. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

The interest on naira and foreign currency remittances is compound interest. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

Any balance of tax unpaid as at the due date attracts interest and penalties as provided in the Act or any other relevant law. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6)]

The relevant tax authority may, for good cause shown, remit the whole or any part of a penalty or interest due under the Act or any other tax law. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 66]

The penalty and interest under section 65 are not treated as part of the tax paid for the purpose of claiming relief under the Act or any other tax law. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The exact naira amount of penalty and interest needs a calculation, which is not done here. It would apply the 10% sum and the interest rate to the tax amount and the period of lateness.
- The interest rate needs the current Central Bank of Nigeria monetary policy rate and the spread set by the Minister. Neither figure is among the passages.
- Section 67, which section 65 refers to, is not among the passages.
- The passages do not say whether the tax was paid in naira or foreign currency, or what the original due date was.
- The passages do not say whether the late payment was a tax that was assessed, withheld or self-accounted, which affects which provisions apply.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65 (gazette pages A 298, A 299)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 49(1) to (6) (gazette pages A 288, A 289)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 66 (gazette page A 299)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65: Interest is SOFR plus 10% or such other spread as the authority determines in the cited text; the National Assembly text says SOFR plus a spread to be determined, without the 10%. (DR-243)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 65: Only the cited text makes the interest in subsection (1)(b) and (c) compound and applies it to tax debts unpaid at commencement. (DR-245)

A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where a person appointed under section 151(3) has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. The remission shall come with a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.
A person with an obligation to collect VAT under Chapter Six of the Act shall keep proper records and make appropriate returns and remittances.

cases.rendered:
Where a non-resident person makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a person appointed under section 151(3) has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

VAT withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. The remission shall come with a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

A person with an obligation to collect VAT under Chapter Six of the Act shall keep proper records and make appropriate returns and remittances. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say whether the Dublin vendor is a non-resident person making taxable supplies, or whether cloud software is a taxable supply.
- The passages do not say whether the Service has appointed the vendor to collect VAT, or whether the vendor has failed to collect it.
- The passages do not say whether the Service has directed the business to self-account.
- Whether the business is a taxable person is not stated in the passages.

Sources

Tax on the total profits of a company for each year of assessment is levied at 0% for a small company and at 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act for any other company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

A small company is a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Under that definition, any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

The 15% minimum effective tax rule applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

The 4% development levy applies to assessable profits of companies chargeable to tax under Chapters Two and Three, other than small companies and non-resident companies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 59]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Whether the juice business counts as gross turnover and total fixed assets within the small company definition is a comparison of the question's figures with the thresholds, which the passages do not make for this company.
- The passages do not say whether making and selling fruit juice is a business providing professional services.
- The passages do not say whether the company's machines and premises count as total fixed assets, or whether the projected turnover is gross turnover.
- The passages do not say whether the company is a constituent entity of an MNE group.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 59 (gazette page A 427)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

My company buys stock from another company I also control. In plain terms, what does section 192 of the NTA expect from us?

A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall ensure that the terms and conditions of the arrangement are at arm's length. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

The company shall also report the arrangement in the form and manner prescribed by the relevant tax authority. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

"Arrangement" includes any agreement, understanding, scheme, financial or commercial relation, transaction or series of transactions. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

"Arm's length terms and conditions" means the terms and conditions obtainable if the transaction or arrangement was between unrelated parties dealing in comparative circumstances. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

Where, in the opinion of a relevant tax authority, a company has entered into an arrangement with a related party that is not at arm's length, the authority may make the necessary adjustments to bring it into line with arm's length terms as provided under the Transfer Pricing Regulations. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

The relevant tax authority may make rules or regulations for the administration of section 192. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 192]

Under the definition of "connected persons", a company is connected to another company where the same person has control over both companies, or connected persons acting separately have control over the companies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "connected persons"]

cases.question: The NRS served us an assessment we believe is wrong. How long do we have to object, and what must our objection contain?

claims.text: A taxable person who disputes a tax assessment may apply to the relevant tax authority for revision and amendment of the assessment, by a written notice of objection delivered in person, by courier service or via electronic means.
An objection is valid only if it is delivered to the relevant tax authority within 30 days from the date of service of the disputed notice of assessment, and it contains the grounds of objection.
The grounds must also state the amendment required to resolve the dispute or correct the error, and the justification for the amendments.
The grounds must also state the amount of assessable and total profits, income or value of transactions admitted by the taxable person for the relevant reporting period.
The grounds must also state the amount of tax admitted by the taxable person, or that no amount of tax is admitted as payable.
Despite the 30-day period, the relevant tax authority may, for any satisfactory and good cause shown, extend the time for making the objection to such reasonable time in the particular circumstances.
On receiving a notice of objection, the relevant tax authority may require the taxable person to furnish particulars and produce books or documents, and may summon any person to give evidence.
The relevant tax authority shall respond to the objection notice within 90 days, otherwise the objection of the taxpayer shall be upheld.

cases.rationale: nta2025:s187 (c) zero-rates educational books (nta2025:s189:def:educational-books); nta2025:s156 (4) says a 0%-rated supplier pays VAT on inputs and may request a refund.
cases.question: We sell school textbooks. Do we charge VAT on them, and can we get back the VAT we pay our printers?

claims.text: VAT is paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act.
Educational books and materials are among the taxable supplies charged to VAT at the rate of 0%. This is subject to paragraph 2 of the Thirtenth Schedule to the Act.

"Educational books" means physical or electronic books used to implement instruction and facilitate learning in educational institutions providing pre-primary, primary, secondary, tertiary, special, adult, vocational, technical science or religious education. The definition includes booklets, brochures, pamphlets and leaflets, newspapers, journals and periodicals, children's books, picture and painting books, music, maps, charts and topographical plans, and covers, cases and other articles supplied together with the books.
A taxable person pays VAT to a supplier on the taxable supply made to that person. The VAT paid is known as input VAT.
A person whose supplies are chargeable to VAT at 0% shall pay VAT on taxable supplies consumed in the production of its supplies, and may thereafter request a refund of the VAT paid.

Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months. The person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not used as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of the information or documents the Service may require.

Input tax on a taxable supply to a registered person may be deducted from the tax payable on its taxable supplies at the end of the tax period in which the supply occurred, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies. Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to taxable supplies may be deducted. The input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred.
The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of the Act.

The passages do not say whether the business's school textbooks fall within the definition of educational books, or whether the printers' services are taxable supplies consumed in producing them.
The passages do not say whether the business is a taxable or registered person.

<question>
We sell school textbooks. Do we charge VAT on them, and can we get back the VAT we pay our printers?
</question>
<gaps>

cases.rendered:
VAT is paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 145]

Educational books and materials are among the taxable supplies charged to VAT at the rate of 0%. This is subject to paragraph 2 of the Thirtenth Schedule to the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 187]

"Educational books" means physical or electronic books used to implement instruction and facilitate learning in educational institutions providing pre-primary, primary, secondary, tertiary, special, adult, vocational, technical science or religious education. The definition includes booklets, brochures, pamphlets and leaflets, newspapers, journals and periodicals, children's books, picture and painting books, music, maps, charts and topographical plans, and covers, cases and other articles supplied together with the books. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 189, definition of "educational books"]

A taxable person pays VAT to a supplier on the taxable supply made to that person. The VAT paid is known as input VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 152]

A person whose supplies are chargeable to VAT at 0% shall pay VAT on taxable supplies consumed in the production of its supplies, and may thereafter request a refund of the VAT paid. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months. The person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not used as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of the information or documents the Service may require. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

Input tax on a taxable supply to a registered person may be deducted from the tax payable on its taxable supplies at the end of the tax period in which the supply occurred, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies. Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to taxable supplies may be deducted. The input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Paragraph 2 of the Thirtenth Schedule, to which section 187 is subject, is not among the passages.
- The passages do not say whether the business's school textbooks fall within the definition of educational books, or whether the printers' services are taxable supplies consumed in producing them.
- The passages do not say whether the business is a taxable or registered person.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 145 (gazette page A 470)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 187 (gazette pages A 490, A 491)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 189, definition of "educational books" (gazette page A 492)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 152 (gazette page A 473)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156 (gazette pages A 474, A 475)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 187: Cross-reference: the gazette refers to paragraph 2 of the 'Thirtenth' Schedule, which has no paragraph 2; the National Assembly text refers to the Tenth Schedule. (DR-081)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 187: The gazette zero-rates electric vehicles and parts and semi-knock-down units for assembling them; the National Assembly text does not list them. (DR-082)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156: The gazette lets a person whose supplies are zero-rated pay VAT on its inputs and then claim a refund; the National Assembly text has no such subsection. (DR-067)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156: Because of the gazette's extra subsection (4), gazette (5) and (6) are National Assembly (4) and (5). (DR-068)

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, or because total profits are less than the dividend declared, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax. This applies whether or not the recipient is a Nigerian company.

The charge is at the rate prescribed in section 56 of the Act, as if the dividend were the total profits of the company for the year of assessment to which the accounts, out of which the dividend is declared, relate.
This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of retained earnings, to the extent the profits or gains in the retained earnings have been taxed under the Act.
This rule does not apply to dividends declared out of profits or gains that are exempt from income tax by the Act.
This rule does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

This rule does not apply to distributions made by a real estate investment company to its shareholders from rental income and dividend income received on behalf of those shareholders, whether paid out of profits of the year in which the dividend is declared or out of profits of previous reporting periods.

gaps: Whether a particular company's dividend falls within an exception, such as retained earnings, exempt profits, franked investment income or a real estate investment company, depends on facts not given.
