Gains accruing to an individual are exempt from tax on the disposal of a dwelling-house, or part of it, or an interest in it. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 51]

The exemption also covers land immediately adjoining the dwelling house, up to a maximum of one acre, but not land used for commercial purposes. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 51]

The exemption is enjoyed once in the lifetime of an individual. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 51]

Where a person disposes of only part of a dwelling-house, or of a house used partly as a dwelling place and partly for a trade, business, profession or vocation, the consideration is apportioned. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 51]

- The passages do not say whether the house in question is the seller's dwelling-house for this exemption, or whether the exemption has already been used.
- The passages do not give the rate of tax or how any taxable part of a gain is worked out; any calculation is not done here.

claims.text: Where a non-resident person makes taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where a person appointed by the Service has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT.
A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. The remittance shall be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.

Federal, State and Local Government bodies and their Ministries, Departments or Agencies, and any other person appointed by the Service, shall collect or withhold VAT on taxable supplies made to them and remit it to the Service.
A foreign company is defined as a non-resident company or any company other than a Nigerian company.

A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a person appointed by the Service has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies are made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. cases.rendered:
A small company is defined as a company that earns gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less per annum with total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000, provided that any business providing professional services shall not be classified as a small company. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company"]

Professional services means services provided by an individual or a firm having specialised knowledge, skills, and qualifications in specific fields, including consulting, planning, or support services, excluding artisans or vocational services. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "professional services"]

A small company is taxed at 0% on total profits for each year of assessment, while any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Whether the particular consulting firm counts as providing professional services on its facts is not stated in the passages.
- Whether the firm is a company is not stated; the definition of small company refers to a company.
- The firm's actual turnover and fixed assets are needed to test the stated thresholds.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company" (gazette page A 510)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "professional services" (gazette page A 508)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less in the gazette and ₦100,000,000 or less in the National Assembly text, which also says 'business' instead of 'company'. (DR-150)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "small company": The gazette excludes any business providing professional services from being a small company; the National Assembly text has no such exclusion. (DR-151)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 202, definition of "professional services": Only the gazette defines 'professional services', the term that excludes a business from being a small company. (DR-138)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)

claims.text: Interest on debt employed in generating the income of a trade, business, profession or vocation is among the deductible expenses, subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule.

Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purpose of Chapter Two.

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is more than 30% of the earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of the Nigerian company in that accounting period.
The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company which is engaged in the business of banking or insurance.

Interest expenditure not wholly deducted for an assessment year is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company and assessable for that year, to the extent permitted by paragraph (2) of the Schedule.
Interest expenditure is not carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed.

Debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession.
No deduction is allowed for any payment to a connected person that is not consistent with the Transfer Pricing Regulations issued by the Service.

cases.rendered:
Interest on debt employed in generating the income of a trade, business, profession or vocation is among the deductible expenses, subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 20(1)(a) to (h)]

Where a Nigerian company or a permanent establishment of a non-resident company in Nigeria incurs interest or similar expenditure on debt issued by a connected person, the excess interest is a disallowable deduction for the purpose of Chapter Two. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

Excess interest means total interest paid or payable to a connected person that is more than 30% of the earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of the Nigerian company in that accounting period. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

The limit does not apply to a Nigerian subsidiary of a foreign company which is engaged in the business of banking or insurance. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

Interest expenditure not wholly deducted for an assessment year is carried forward to the following assessment year or years. It is allowed against the profits, if any, of any business carried on by the company and assessable for that year, to the extent permitted by paragraph (2) of the Schedule. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

Interest expenditure is not carried forward for more than five assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the excess interest expenditure was first computed. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

Debt means any loan, financial instrument, finance lease, financial derivative, or any arrangement that gives rise to interest, discounts or other finance charges that are deductible in computing income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, Third Schedule]

No deduction is allowed for any payment to a connected person that is not consistent with the Transfer Pricing Regulations issued by the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 21(a) to (o)]

claims.text: Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the taxable person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged.
The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment, where the tax audit began before the six-year limit expired.

Despite the time limit, where a taxable person makes a deliberate misstatement in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as necessary, assess the taxable person to the amount or additional amount needed to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement.

All relevant facts are to be considered in working out the additional amount of tax, even where those facts were not known when an earlier assessment or additional assessment was made for the same year.

The tax authority is not prevented from making an assessment or additional assessment for a year, where this does not involve re-opening any issue on the same facts that was already determined for that year of assessment by agreement or on appeal under section 41(5).

cases.rendered:
Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the taxable person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 36]

The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment, where the tax audit began before the six-year limit expired. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 36]

Despite the time limit, where a taxable person makes a deliberate misstatement in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as necessary, assess the taxable person to the amount or additional amount needed to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 36]

All relevant facts are to be considered in working out the additional amount of tax, even where those facts were not known when an earlier assessment or additional assessment was made for the same year. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 36]

The tax authority is not prevented from making an assessment or additional assessment for a year, where this does not involve re-opening any issue on the same facts that was already determined for that year of assessment by agreement or on appeal under section 41(5). [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 43]

- The passages do not say how the six years are counted beyond the words 'within six years of the assessment', and no dates are worked out here.

claims.text: Where a business produces no assessable profit, or an assessable profit less than expected from that business, or the true amount of the assessable profit cannot be readily ascertained, the relevant tax authority may act under the deemed profit rule.

cases.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%. Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of this Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule.

A company includes dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax.

Where the effective tax rate of a company in a year of assessment is less than 15%, the company must recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%. This applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.

Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%. Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of this Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4)]

A company includes dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8]

Where the effective tax rate of a company in a year of assessment is less than 15%, the company must recompute and pay an additional tax that makes its effective tax rate equal to 15%. This applies to a company that is a constituent entity of an MNE group, and to any other company with an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not define a small company, so whether the company is a small company at 0% or another company at 30 per cent cannot be determined.
- The question does not say whether the stated profit is total profits after losses and capital allowances. The calculation of tax on it is not done here.
- The company's turnover and whether it is part of an MNE group are not given, so whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies cannot be determined.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 412, A 413)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8 (gazette page A 397)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.question: Under section 191 of the Nigeria Tax Act, where do objections and appeals go?

claims.text: Under section 191, a relevant tax authority that thinks a transaction reducing or likely to reduce tax payable is artificial or fictitious may disregard it, or direct adjustments to liability to tax, and issue an assessment or additional assessment.
The provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under section 191.
Where the taxable person and the relevant tax authority do not agree on the amount of tax, or the authority treats the objection notice as invalid, the taxpayer may exercise the right of appeal.
A party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may appeal to the Court of Appeal, and an appeal against the Court of Appeal's judgement goes to the Supreme Court.

cases.rendered:
Under section 191, a relevant tax authority that thinks a transaction reducing or likely to reduce tax payable is artificial or fictitious may disregard it, or direct adjustments to liability to tax, and issue an assessment or additional assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191]

The provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under section 191. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191]

Where the taxable person and the relevant tax authority do not agree on the amount of tax, or the authority treats the objection notice as invalid, the taxpayer may exercise the right of appeal. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8)]

A party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may appeal to the Court of Appeal, and an appeal against the Court of Appeal's judgement goes to the Supreme Court. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, which section 191 names, is not among the passages, so the question of where objections and appeals go under that chapter cannot be fully answered.
- The passages do not say which body hears the first appeal before the High Court.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191 (gazette page A 497)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8) (gazette page A 285)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8): The Gombe print requires a taxpayer appealing from the Tax Appeal Tribunal to the High Court to pay 20% of the disputed amount first; the cited print has no deposit clause, and Gombe's (9) is its (8). (DR-229)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8): The cited print's s41(8) provides appeals from the High Court to the Court of Appeal and then the Supreme Court; the National Assembly text has no such subsection. (DR-231)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191: As printed, section 191(2) refers objections and appeals to Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025. In the cited NRS print of that Act, Chapter Four is Offences and Penalties; objections are in Chapter Two (section 41), which Nigeria Tax Act section 10(7) cites. (DQ-16)
